nama_domain: AI & Labor Automation (state-driven AI diffusion causing white-collar displacement, entry-level job collapse, and 'quiet layoffs')
kategori: Ketenagakerjaan (Labor & Employment) - with strong spillovers into Education Policy, Industrial Policy, and Social Protection
tahun_mulai_china: Two distinct waves. (1) BLUE-COLLAR automation wave: began ~2013-2016 (Made in China 2025 issued May 2015; Foxconn replaced 60,000 workers with robots at its Kunshan plant in 2016; China became the world's largest industrial robot market from 2013). (2) WHITE-COLLAR / GENERATIVE-AI wave — the subject of this research: began late 2022-early 2023 with ChatGPT, accelerated decisively in Jan-Feb 2025 with DeepSeek-R1 (which made frontier-grade models cheap enough for mass domestic enterprise deployment), and became explicit state policy on 27 August 2025 when the State Council issued the 'AI+' (人工智能+) Action Plan. The employment shock became publicly measurable in H1 2025 (graduate job postings -22% YoY) and a formal government policy problem on 27 January 2026, when MOHRSS announced China would issue a dedicated document on 'responding to the impact of AI and promoting employment' (应对人工智能影响促就业).
pemain_kunci_china: STATE ACTORS: State Council (issuer of the 'AI+' Action Plan, 27 Aug 2025); Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS / 人社部) — Minister Wang Xiaoping, announced the AI-employment policy document on 27 Jan 2026 and runs the unemployment-risk monitoring system; MIIT (Vice-Minister Zhang Yunming: 'restructuring is not disappearance, iteration is not replacement'); National Development and Reform Commission; Central Party School (Study Times, Nov 2025, floated legislation on AI-driven displacement); All-China Federation of Trade Unions. MODEL/PLATFORM COMPANIES: DeepSeek (whose Nov 2025 statement that AI success means 'replacing the vast majority of human jobs' triggered national debate), Alibaba (Qwen; 'Wukong' one-person-company automation platform; ~34% headcount reduction in 2025), Tencent, ByteDance (Doubao), Baidu (Ernie; ~7% headcount down by end-2025), Moonshot/Kimi, Zhipu AI, MiniMax, iFlytek. INDUSTRIAL AUTOMATION: Foxconn, BYD (~100,000 jobs cut in 2025, ~10%), Xiaomi (Changping 'dark factory'), Midea, Haier, Estun/Siasun/Inovance (domestic robot makers), Unitree (humanoids). LABOR-MARKET INFRASTRUCTURE: Zhaopin (智联招聘) and BOSS Zhipi (BOSS直聘) — the recruitment platforms whose data made the entry-level collapse visible; MyCOS (麦可思) for graduate-employment tracking. EDUCATION: Ministry of Education (2026 undergraduate major catalogue; 600+ universities with AI undergraduate programs).
apa_yang_terjadi_di_china:
China is running the world's first deliberate, state-orchestrated, economy-wide AI diffusion program while simultaneously discovering that the same program is the main threat to its most politically sensitive metric — youth employment. The mechanism has five interlocking parts.

(1) TOP-DOWN DIFFUSION MANDATE. The State Council's 'AI+' Action Plan (27 Aug 2025) sets hard numeric penetration targets — next-generation intelligent terminals and AI agents to exceed 70% penetration by 2027, 90% by 2030, with a fully 'intelligent society' by 2035 — across six domains: science & technology, industry, consumption, public welfare, governance, and international cooperation. The 2026 Government Work Report wrote 'intelligent agents' (智能体) into policy text for the first time. This is not a market outcome that the state is reacting to; it is a target the state is pushing enterprises and SOEs to hit, with provincial governments and SASAC-supervised SOEs graded on adoption.

(2) CHEAP MODELS MADE DIFFUSION REAL. DeepSeek's early-2025 releases collapsed inference costs domestically, so AI agent deployment stopped being a big-tech luxury and became affordable for mid-size firms and even individual contractors. Chinese enterprise AI-agent deployment reached roughly 79% of surveyed enterprises with ~23% at full production scale, with penetration above 30% in finance and e-commerce and near 20% in manufacturing.

(3) DISPLACEMENT SHOWS UP FIRST AT THE ENTRY LEVEL, NOT AS MASS LAYOFFS. Chinese labor law requires government approval for layoffs exceeding 10% of a workforce, and Beijing has reportedly directed large tech firms to avoid visible mass layoffs. The result is 'quiet layoffs' (隐形裁员): attrition without backfill, performance-management exits, forced internal transfers, contractor non-renewal, and above all a freeze on entry-level hiring. Alibaba's headcount fell about 34% in 2025; Baidu's by nearly 7%; BYD cut roughly 100,000 (≈10%); nearly half of listed Chinese firms reduced headcount in 2025; aggregate employment growth at listed companies fell from 6.4% (2021) to 1% (2024), recovering only to 1.9% (2025). Micro-drama and content studios report departments shrinking from 30-40 people to about 10 after AI adoption. A fintech firm largely replaced marketing and front-end roles with AI.

(4) THE BURDEN LANDS ON FRESH GRADUATES. Zhaopin data show job postings targeting new graduates fell 22% in H1 2025 while the number of graduate job-seekers rose 8% — a scissors gap arriving exactly as record cohorts graduate (12.22 million in 2025, ~12.7 million in 2026). Youth (16-24, excluding students) unemployment hit 16.3% in April 2026, near record. Citi estimates 9.6% of all Chinese jobs (~70 million) are at high risk of AI displacement, rising to 13.6% for workers in their 20s. Paradoxically, AI-related job postings surged 74% in 2025 — the new jobs are real but are senior/technical and far fewer than the entry-level rungs being removed. The displaced flow downward into the 280-million-strong flexible/gig economy: cities have run subsidy schemes paying new graduates up to ~29,000 yuan to take food-delivery work, and a graduate can earn ~160 yuan on a good delivery day against ~93,190 yuan/year for an average office worker.

(5) THE STATE IS NOW BUILDING A LABOR-SIDE COUNTERWEIGHT. Beijing's position, articulated by MIIT, is 'human-machine coordination' (人机协同) — restructuring, not elimination. Concretely: Chinese labor arbitration and courts have already ruled in at least three cases that adopting AI is NOT lawful grounds for termination; a Beijing arbitration decision in December 2025 required employers to consider contract modification, retraining, and internal transfer first, and one worker was awarded 260,000 yuan (~US$38,000) for an unlawful AI-substitution dismissal. On 27 January 2026 MOHRSS announced a forthcoming national document on responding to AI's employment impact, bundled with a 'stabilize-expand-upgrade employment' action, sectoral employment-support measures, a dedicated graduate/youth employment document, basic-rights protection measures for new-form employment workers, and an interim regulation on over-age workers. Proposals under discussion include AI-specific unemployment insurance, 6-12 month grace periods before AI-driven layoffs take effect, mandatory upskilling funding, and regional employment-monitoring pilots. China is therefore attempting something novel: maximum-speed AI adoption plus administratively suppressed layoffs, absorbing the slack through SOEs, gig work, civil-service exam demand, and delayed labor-market entry via graduate school.
data_skala_china:
AI DIFFUSION TARGETS & MARKET. 'AI+' Action Plan (State Council, 27 Aug 2025): AI agent + next-gen intelligent terminal penetration >70% by 2027, >90% by 2030; intelligent society by 2035. China's AI-agent industry market size ~182.34 billion yuan in 2025, +78.03% YoY (Guanyan Report); enterprise-grade AI agent market variously estimated at 86bn yuan (2024) → 212bn yuan (2025) → 449bn yuan (2026F), CAGR ~107%; projections to 852bn yuan by 2028 and >3.32 trillion yuan by 2029 [uncertain — vendor/consultancy estimates diverge widely]. Enterprise adoption: ~79% of surveyed enterprises have deployed AI agents, ~23% at full production scale; sector penetration >30% finance and e-commerce, ~20% manufacturing.

LABOR MARKET. Total workforce ~725 million; white-collar positions are less than 25% of that. Graduate job postings -22% YoY in H1 2025 (Zhaopin) while graduate job-seekers +8%. Record graduate cohorts: 12.22 million (2025, +430,000 YoY); ~12.7 million (2026). Youth (16-24, ex-students) unemployment 16.3% in April 2026, near record high. Urban surveyed unemployment stable at ~5% (target 5.5%); ~3 million new urban jobs in Q1 2026 against a 12-million annual target. Citi: 9.6% of Chinese jobs (~70 million) at high AI-displacement risk; 13.6% for workers in their 20s. AI-related job postings +74% in 2025. Entry-level postings on BOSS Zhipin held roughly steady at ~7% of listings — one of the main contradictions in the data.

CORPORATE HEADCOUNT (2025 annual reports, filed end-March 2026). Alibaba: ~-34%. Baidu: ~-7%. BYD: ~-10% (~100,000 jobs). Tencent: +5% (115,849 staff). Nearly 50% of listed Chinese firms reduced headcount in 2025. Listed-company employment growth: 6.4% (2021) → 1.0% (2024) → 1.9% (2025).

BLUE-COLLAR / ROBOTICS BASELINE. Manufacturing workforce fell from ~115 million (2013) to below ~85 million (2025) — over 30 million jobs lost — even as exports hit records. Over 2 million operational factory robots in 2024 (IFR World Robotics 2025), ~54% of global demand; robot density ~392-400+ per 10,000 manufacturing workers (2023-2025) vs global average 141. China has invested >US$15 billion in advanced-manufacturing retraining since 2020 [uncertain — single-source Bloomberg-attributed figure].

ABSORPTION CHANNELS. Flexible/gig employment ~280 million, nearly 40% of the urban workforce. 'AI anxiety' hashtag on RedNote/Xiaohongshu: ~7.8 million views. Wage anchors: average office worker 93,190 yuan/yr (~US$13,700); engineering roles quoted as low as ~100,000 yuan/yr; entry-level delivery ~160 yuan on a good day; municipal subsidies up to 29,000 yuan for graduates entering delivery work.

EDUCATION RESTRUCTURING. 600+ universities offer AI undergraduate programs by 2026, up from 35 approved in 2018. 2021-2025: ~12,200 undergraduate degree programs ended or suspended; ~10,200 new ones introduced. MOE 2026 catalogue adds 38 new undergraduate majors (AI for business, embodied intelligence, brain-computer science & technology, data intelligence, low-altitude economy management, semiconductor equipment engineering, rare-earth science); 9 universities authorized for 'embodied intelligence'. A May 2026 survey of 70 universities found 8 Japanese-language majors, 5 German majors, and 5 translation programs eliminated.
fase_tren_di_china: BOOMING on the technology/diffusion side, simultaneously entering EARLY REGULATED/BACKLASH on the labor side — a rare split-phase condition. Diffusion is in a state-accelerated boom (2025-2027 target window, 70% agent penetration by 2027). Labor impact has moved through emerging (2023-2024) → visible and contested (2025, graduate posting collapse, 'quiet layoffs', DeepSeek's 'replace most jobs' remark) → into the pre-regulatory phase (Dec 2025 arbitration precedent; 27 Jan 2026 MOHRSS announcement of a dedicated AI-employment document). Notably, China is regulating the LABOR consequences of AI without slowing AI ADOPTION — the opposite sequencing from its platform-economy crackdown (2020-2022), where the state slowed the industry itself. Expect 2026-2028 to be the 'managed displacement' phase: mandatory retraining, layoff grace periods, judicial hostility to AI-substitution dismissals, SOE absorption, and expanded unemployment insurance, all layered on top of an unchanged 90%-by-2030 adoption target.
puncak_tren_china: Not yet reached. The DIFFUSION peak is targeted by policy at 2027 (70% agent penetration) with saturation around 2030 (90%) and the declared 'intelligent society' endpoint at 2035. The LABOR-PAIN peak is most likely 2026-2029: the collision of the largest-ever graduate cohorts (12.7m+ per year), the 2027 penetration deadline forcing accelerated enterprise deployment, and the exhaustion of gig-economy absorption capacity (dozens of cities have already issued ride-hailing 'capacity saturation warnings'). Geographically the epicentre is the tier-1 white-collar clusters — Beijing (Zhongguancun, content/marketing/internet HQs), Hangzhou (Alibaba, DeepSeek, the '6 Little Dragons'), Shenzhen (Tencent, BYD, hardware), Shanghai (finance, professional services), plus Guangdong/Jiangsu/Zhejiang for the parallel manufacturing-automation wave. Sectorally the first casualties are internet content operations, marketing/copywriting, customer service, junior programming/testing, translation, basic graphic design, junior financial analysis, and back-office administration. [uncertain — peak timing is a projection, not an observed fact]
status_di_indonesia: BARU MULAI / EARLY ENTRY WITH A DIFFERENT MECHANISM. AI-attributed layoffs and hiring freezes have begun in Indonesia's tech, e-commerce, BPO-adjacent, and creative sectors, and AI agents are commercially available and being deployed (banking, e-commerce, logistics). But unlike China there is no state diffusion mandate, no numeric penetration target, and no evidence yet of economy-wide white-collar displacement. Population-level AI adoption is only ~18.2% (APJII 2026) and organizational AI implementation ~26%. Indonesia is roughly at China's 2023-2024 stage on displacement, but is AHEAD of most peers on individual worker AI usage (33% of Indonesian workers classed as 'Frontier Professionals', more than double the global average of 16% — Microsoft Work Trend Index 2026) and is moving on regulation earlier in the cycle than China did (draft AI Perpres 2026, DPR Commission IX explicitly demanding AI-displacement clauses in the Labor Law revision).
contoh_konkret_indonesia: LAYOFFS & RESTRUCTURING: Tokopedia under ByteDance — four rounds of cuts since operational control (≈450 in June 2024, ≈180 in July 2025, ≈240 in August 2025, ~200 accepting packages in July 2026), with the July 2026 '90% layoff' rumour triggering direct government intervention after the Tokopedia Lite launch; GoTo (1,300 in 2022; 600 in March 2023); Bukalapak (<5% of workforce, Aug 2023); Shopee and Lazada framing cuts as a shift from growth to productivity with investment redirected to AI. Global employers cutting Indonesian-relevant white-collar work: Accenture (AI made data analysis, system testing, report preparation more efficient, reducing entry/mid-level need), Salesforce (Einstein absorbing routine customer communication, support docs, daily content). AI AGENT DEPLOYMENT: a national logistics firm in Surabaya reports ~75% of document verification, delivery scheduling, and customer-complaint handling running without human intervention on an AI-agent platform; AI-agent subscriptions from Rp1-2 million/month with ready-made WhatsApp agents now within reach of mid-size UMKM. BANKING: Bank Mandiri applies AI to business improvement, operational efficiency, and operational risk, with ~4,500 staff in its IT directorate — but explicitly states headcount reduction is not under consideration near-term; state banks (BRI, Mandiri, BNI) remain a job-stability anchor, so no visible AI-driven banking layoff wave yet. CHINA-LINKED TRANSMISSION: Alibaba Cloud AI Talent Development Program roadshows in 9 cities (Jakarta, Bandung, Yogyakarta, Malang, Makassar, Aceh, Padang, Bali, Papua), 60+ communities/universities, 500+ participants, 500+ cloud certifications, pushing Qwen LLM and Wan video-generation models into the local creative industry; Telkom AI Center of Excellence (launched 2025) partnering with Alibaba Cloud on AI talent; Huawei Partner Summit 2026 building an Indonesian AI partner ecosystem. INFRASTRUCTURE: Nvidia-Indosat US$200 million AI centre; Nvidia-backed AI hub in Batam; Microsoft US$1.7 billion cloud/AI commitment and Indonesia Central Cloud Region; DAMAC Digital US$2.3 billion Jakarta data centre; pipeline of ~1.3 GW of planned data-centre capacity on top of ~580 MW operating. EDUCATION: Universitas Indonesia's Fasilkom AI undergraduate program approved by Academic Senate 3 Oct 2025, first intake 2026/2027, ~16 designated lecturers; ITS Rekayasa Kecerdasan Artifisial; BINUS and UPH AI programs. POLICY: Komdigi's National AI Roadmap White Paper (public consultation Aug 2025) and two draft Presidential Regulations (National AI Roadmap 2026-2030 and AI Ethics/Governance) targeted for Q1 2026 — reportedly without sanctions, prioritising governance and public trust; Kemnaker using AI itself for labour-market analysis and training planning (webinar 17 July 2026, Secretary-General Cris Kuntadi); DPR Commission IX member Pulung Agustanto arguing the Labor Law revision must protect workers from automation and AI; Apindo pushing the RUU Ketenagakerjaan toward job creation and layoff prevention.
data_skala_indonesia:
LABOR MARKET (BPS, February 2026 Sakernas). Total unemployed 7.24 million (one report cites 7.35 million for a later reference period [uncertain]); national open unemployment rate (TPT) 4.68%. Tertiary graduates (D4/S1/S2/S3): TPT 6.13%, i.e. 1,033,737 unemployed — up 23,085 YoY even as total national unemployment FELL by 34,702, and up ~338,433 (+48.7%) versus February 2016. Youth (15-24) unemployment 16.36% — almost identical to China's 16.3%. NEET: ~8.9 million (5.7 million aged 20-24; 3.2 million aged 15-19). Informal employment 57.70% of workers; formal workers 59.93 million (up from 59.19 million a year earlier); 47.42 million (32.06% of the employed) are non-full-time.

LAYOFFS. Kemnaker: >88,000 workers laid off during 2025; 23,470 in January-May 2026. Indonesian media count >160,000 technology-sector workers laid off by mid-2026 as firms restructured around AI [uncertain — this figure appears to conflate global tech-sector layoffs reported by trackers with Indonesian-specific layoffs; treat as indicative, not national data].

AI ADOPTION. General population AI adoption 18.2% (APJII 2026 internet penetration & behaviour survey). Organizational AI implementation ~26% (Pertama Partners SEA Mid-Market AI Adoption Index 2026); 23% of enterprises in the AI 'investment' stage interoperating with business functions (IBM/Advisia study). Worker-level: 33% of Indonesian workers are 'Frontier Professionals' vs 16% globally (Microsoft Work Trend Index 2026); 69% used AI for their role in the past year but only 16% use generative AI daily (PwC Hopes & Fears 2025).

CREATIVE SECTOR DAMAGE. Roughly 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators report having lost work because of generative AI [uncertain — the underlying survey population and whether it is Indonesia-specific is not clearly established; possibly an international figure circulated in Indonesian media].

INFRASTRUCTURE & TALENT. AI-optimised data centre market US$0.66bn (2025) → US$1.44bn (2030F), CAGR 16.91%; broader data-centre market projected US$6.08bn by 2031 across 88 existing and 25 upcoming facilities in 17 cities; ~1.3 GW planned capacity vs ~580 MW operating; up to US$20bn of data-centre investment lined up. Digital talent: need for 9 million by 2030 against roughly 500,000 today, with universities supplying only ~100,000-200,000/year — a shortfall of 400,000-500,000 per year.

STRUCTURAL CONTEXT. GDP per capita ~US$5,362 (2026 nominal) vs China's ~US$13,866 (2025) — about 39%. Internet penetration 81.72% (235.3 million of 287.3 million people, APJII 2026) — actually slightly ABOVE China's 80.1%. Urbanisation ~60.3% vs China ~66%.
estimasi_lag_tahun:
2-4 YEARS on displacement impact, but effectively 5-8 YEARS (or never, in the same form) on state-driven diffusion intensity. Decomposed:
- AI TOOL ACCESS / INDIVIDUAL USE: ~0-1 year lag, arguably ZERO. Indonesian workers use frontier AI at more than double the global rate, internet penetration exceeds China's, and the same foundation models (GPT, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek) are available the day they ship. This dimension is effectively simultaneous.
- ENTERPRISE AI-AGENT DEPLOYMENT AT SCALE: ~3-4 years. Chinese enterprises are at ~79% deployment / ~23% full production; Indonesia is at ~23-26% organizational implementation — roughly where China was in 2023.
- MEASURABLE ENTRY-LEVEL WHITE-COLLAR DISPLACEMENT: ~2-3 years. China's -22% graduate-posting shock landed in H1 2025; Indonesia's tertiary-graduate unemployment is already rising against a falling national trend (Feb 2026), which looks like the leading edge of the same phenomenon arriving 2027-2028 with force.
- STATE DIFFUSION MANDATE: 5-10 years or never. Indonesia has no equivalent to a State Council penetration target; its AI Perpres is reportedly sanction-free and governance-oriented.
- LABOR-PROTECTION REGULATION: near-zero lag, possibly NEGATIVE (Indonesia earlier). China announced its AI-employment document in Jan 2026; Indonesia's DPR was debating AI clauses in the Labor Law revision by mid-2026. Indonesia may regulate the labor side BEFORE experiencing the shock — an unusual and potentially advantageous position.
Overall best single estimate: 3 years on impact, with very high variance by sector.
bukti_historical_lag:
Cross-trend calibration from this research series and adjacent evidence:
(1) E-COMMERCE / SOCIAL COMMERCE: China's livestream commerce exploded 2019-2021; Indonesia's TikTok Shop wave landed 2021-2023 — a 2-3 year lag, and closed FASTER than earlier trends because the transmission was a Chinese platform entering directly rather than local imitation.
(2) FINTECH / QR PAYMENTS: Alipay/WeChat Pay reached mass adoption ~2015-2017; QRIS launched 2019-2020 and reached mass adoption ~2022-2023 — a 4-6 year lag, but with a leapfrog element (Indonesia built an interoperable national standard rather than replicating a duopoly).
(3) PLATFORM GIG ECONOMY: Meituan/Didi scale 2015-2017; Gojek/Grab scale 2017-2019 — only a ~2 year lag, because the business model transferred through venture capital and direct competition.
(4) INDUSTRIAL ROBOTICS: this is where the lag is LARGEST and most instructive. China passed 392+ robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers by 2023; Indonesia's robot density remains in the low tens [uncertain — precise IFR figure for Indonesia not retrieved]. Indonesia never experienced China's 2013-2025 manufacturing-employment collapse (115m → <85m) because it never built the automatable manufacturing base. This is direct evidence that CAPITAL-INTENSIVE automation transfers slowly to Indonesia while SOFTWARE-BASED automation transfers fast.
(5) THE KEY ASYMMETRY: generative AI is software delivered over the internet at near-zero marginal cost, in contrast to every prior trend that required capital deployment, logistics, or regulatory licences. Indonesia's internet penetration (81.72%) already EXCEEDS China's (80.1%), and Indonesian workers out-adopt the global average on frontier AI use. Historical lag estimates derived from capital-intensive trends will therefore OVERSTATE the lag for AI-driven white-collar displacement. The binding constraint in Indonesia is not access to AI — it is the small size of the white-collar workforce that AI can displace.
tipe_lag: MIXED — LAGGARD on state-driven diffusion and enterprise-scale deployment (3-4 years behind), SIMULTANEOUS on individual/worker-level AI use and model access (0-1 year), and potentially REVERSE on labor-protection regulation (Indonesia is debating AI-displacement clauses in its Labor Law revision at roughly the same time China announced its first AI-employment document, and before the shock has fully landed). There is also a genuine LEAPFROG risk in the negative direction: because Indonesia has a much thinner white-collar layer and a much thicker informal economy, AI may skip the 'orderly white-collar restructuring' phase China is managing and instead directly choke the entry-level rungs that Indonesian graduates use to enter the formal economy — displacement without the compensating industrial upgrade.
probabilitas_transfer: TINGGI (HIGH) — for the technology and for entry-level white-collar displacement. SEDANG-RENDAH (MEDIUM-LOW) for the specific Chinese form (state-mandated penetration targets + administratively suppressed layoffs + SOE absorption).
alasan_probabilitas:
HIGH-probability drivers: (a) Generative AI is delivered as software over the internet — no ports, no factories, no import licences, no physical logistics; the same models Chinese firms use are available in Jakarta on release day. (b) Indonesia's internet penetration (81.72%) already exceeds China's (80.1%) and 33% of Indonesian workers are advanced AI users versus a 16% global average — the demand-side conditions are already met. (c) The transmission is already underway through multinational employers (Accenture, Salesforce), platform owners restructuring around AI (ByteDance/Tokopedia, Shopee, Lazada), and Chinese cloud vendors actively selling agents (Alibaba Cloud's Qwen and Wan models, 9-city roadshows, Telkom AI CoE partnership; Huawei's 2026 partner ecosystem build). (d) AI-agent pricing has already fallen to Rp1-2 million/month — inside the budget of Indonesian UMKM, meaning diffusion does not depend on large-enterprise capex. (e) Indonesia's tertiary-graduate unemployment is ALREADY rising (+23,085 YoY, Feb 2026) against falling national unemployment — the entry-level squeeze has structurally begun even before AI is the dominant cause.

Why the CHINESE FORM transfers only partially: (i) There is no Indonesian analogue to a State Council document setting a 70%-by-2027 penetration target, and the draft AI Perpres is reportedly sanction-free and governance-focused rather than a diffusion mandate. (ii) China's suppression mechanism — layoffs above 10% requiring government approval, courts ruling AI substitution an unlawful ground for dismissal, SOEs instructed to absorb surplus labour — depends on state capacity over the corporate sector that Indonesia does not possess; the Cipta Kerja framework made severance cheaper and dismissal easier, so Indonesian displacement will be more visible and faster, not quieter. (iii) China's displacement is happening inside a large, formal, white-collar economy (though still under 25% of its 725m workforce); in Indonesia 57.70% of workers are informal and the automatable white-collar layer is proportionally much smaller — so the absolute number displaced will be far lower, but the damage will be concentrated on precisely the group Indonesia is counting on for mobility: urban tertiary graduates. (iv) Indonesia lacks China's absorption channels — no comparable SOE hiring capacity, no civil-service exam absorbing millions, no municipal subsidy programs paying graduates to enter delivery work.
vektor_transmisi:
(a) DIRECT ENTRY BY GLOBAL AND CHINESE PLAYERS — the dominant vector. Chinese cloud/AI vendors are selling agent capability into Indonesia now: Alibaba Cloud is running an AI Talent Development Program across 9 cities (Jakarta, Bandung, Yogyakarta, Malang, Makassar, Aceh, Padang, Bali, Papua) with 60+ communities and universities, 500+ certifications, pushing the Qwen LLM family plus Wan/'Happy Horse' video-generation models explicitly aimed at the creative industry — i.e. selling the exact tool that displaces Indonesian illustrators and video editors; Huawei's Partner Summit 2026 is assembling an Indonesian AI partner ecosystem; DeepSeek's open-weight models are freely deployable by any Indonesian firm. Simultaneously ByteDance controls Tokopedia and is restructuring it around AI-driven efficiency, and Western vendors (Microsoft US$1.7bn, Nvidia-Indosat US$200m, DAMAC US$2.3bn) are building the compute substrate.

(b) EMPLOYER-SIDE POLICY IMPORT VIA MULTINATIONALS AND GCCs — Accenture, Salesforce and similar firms make global decisions to cut entry and mid-level roles after AI adoption, and those decisions propagate to Indonesian delivery centres and back-offices without any local deliberation. This is the fastest and least visible vector.

(c) LOCAL COPYCAT / SaaS RESELLING — Indonesian AI-agent vendors packaging foreign models into WhatsApp-native agents at Rp1-2m/month for UMKM; the Surabaya logistics case (75% of document verification, scheduling, and complaint handling automated) is the template being sold to every mid-size Indonesian firm.

(d) ALGORITHMIC CONTENT DIFFUSION — Chinese-origin AI narratives, tools, and 'one-person company' workflows spread through TikTok, Xiaohongshu-derived content, and Indonesian tech media; Alibaba's 'Wukong' one-person-company automation concept is a directly copyable playbook for Indonesian solopreneurs, which accelerates both productivity and the hollowing-out of junior support roles.

(e) CHINESE VENTURE CAPITAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE — less central here than in e-commerce or fintech, but relevant through data-centre and cloud-region investment that lowers local inference cost.

(f) DIASPORA / ALUMNI AND TALENT PROGRAMS — Indonesian graduates of Chinese universities, Alibaba Cloud/Huawei certification alumni, and Telkom's AI Center of Excellence trainees carry Chinese-style AI deployment practices into Indonesian corporates.

(g) POLICY EMULATION — Indonesia's Komdigi roadmap and Kemnaker's own AI-based labour-market analysis show the state is watching the Chinese and global playbooks; the risk is importing the ADOPTION target while omitting the LABOR-PROTECTION counterweight.
prasyarat_struktural:
WHAT MUST BE TRUE FOR THE CHINESE PATTERN TO ARRIVE, AND WHERE INDONESIA STANDS:

1) INTERNET / DIGITAL SUBSTRATE — threshold: >75% penetration. China at 'AI+' launch (2025): 80.1%. Indonesia (2026): 81.72%, 235.3m users. STATUS: MET AND EXCEEDED. This is the single most important reason the lag will be shorter than for any previous China trend.

2) A LARGE ENOUGH WHITE-COLLAR / FORMAL SERVICES LAYER TO DISPLACE — China: white-collar <25% of a 725m workforce, i.e. roughly 150-180m people, inside a formal economy. Indonesia: informal employment 57.70%; formal workers 59.93m; only ~1.03m unemployed tertiary graduates but a tertiary-educated workforce far smaller in share. STATUS: PARTIALLY MET, MUCH SMALLER. This caps the absolute scale of displacement but concentrates it on the urban graduate class.

3) INCOME LEVEL WHERE LABOUR COST EXCEEDS AI COST — the decisive economic threshold. China's GDP per capita at 'AI+' launch: ~US$13,866; average office salary ~93,190 yuan (~US$13,700/yr) — automating that worker saves real money. Indonesia (2026): GDP per capita ~US$5,362, about 39% of China's; entry-level white-collar salaries in Jakarta are a fraction of Chinese equivalents. STATUS: NOT MET AT THE SAME MARGIN. Cheap human labour is Indonesia's structural brake on AI substitution — but that brake WEAKENS every year as inference costs fall faster than Indonesian wages rise. The crossover for routine admin/CS work is plausibly 2027-2029.

4) ENTERPRISE DIGITAL MATURITY (cloud, structured data, workflow digitisation) — agents cannot automate processes that are not digitised. China: ~79% enterprise agent deployment, ~23% at full production. Indonesia: ~23-26% organizational implementation, only 16% daily generative-AI use among workers despite 69% having tried it. STATUS: NOT MET — this is the true 3-4 year gap.

5) COMPUTE / DATA-CENTRE CAPACITY AND LOCAL INFERENCE COST — Indonesia: ~580 MW operating, ~1.3 GW planned, up to US$20bn of announced investment, Microsoft cloud region live, Nvidia-Indosat and Batam hubs. STATUS: IN PROGRESS, adequate for agent workloads by ~2027.

hambatan_transfer:
1) WAGE ARBITRAGE RUNS THE OTHER WAY. Indonesian white-collar wages are low enough that the ROI on replacing an admin clerk or CS agent with an AI agent is far weaker than in China. At GDP per capita ~39% of China's, the automation payback period is roughly 2-3x longer. This is the strongest single brake.
2) LOW ENTERPRISE DIGITAL MATURITY. Agents automate digitised workflows; Indonesian mid-market firms still run on spreadsheets, WhatsApp, and paper. Only ~23-26% of organizations have implemented AI and only 16% of workers use generative AI daily despite 69% having tried it — the gap between trial and embedded process use is the real barrier.
3) SEVERE AI/DATA TALENT SHORTAGE. 9 million digital talents needed by 2030 versus ~500,000 today and 100,000-200,000 produced per year. Firms cannot deploy agents they cannot configure, integrate, or govern.
4) NO STATE DIFFUSION MANDATE. Without a State Council-style 70%/90% target, Indonesian adoption is left to individual firm ROI calculations, which are unfavourable in the near term.
5) LANGUAGE AND DATA THINNESS. Bahasa Indonesia and especially regional languages (Javanese, Sundanese, Minang, Bugis) are under-represented in training data; domain data for Indonesian regulation, tax, and legal contexts is scarce, so agent accuracy in local workflows lags English/Mandarin performance.
6) ELECTRICITY AND INFRASTRUCTURE CONSTRAINTS. Only ~580 MW of data-centre capacity operating; grid reliability and power cost outside Java constrain local inference.
7) LABOUR-RELATIONS FRICTION AND POLITICAL SENSITIVITY. PHK is politically explosive in Indonesia; the government intervened within days over an unverified Tokopedia rumour. Firms have strong incentives to avoid AI-attributed layoffs becoming a public story, which pushes displacement into slow hiring freezes rather than visible cuts.
8) SME/UMKM STRUCTURE. Indonesia's economy is dominated by ~65 million MSMEs, most micro and family-run, with no formal white-collar staff to displace and limited capacity to adopt agents beyond a WhatsApp chatbot.
9) TRUST, SECURITY AND DATA-PROTECTION UNCERTAINTY. UU PDP implementation, unclear liability rules, and the sanction-free draft Perpres leave enterprises hesitant on customer-facing autonomous agents.
10) INTERNAL RESISTANCE AND SKILL GAPS ACROSS GENERATIONS. PwC's Indonesian findings show a productivity boost concentrated in Gen Z with persistent skill gaps across older cohorts — the people who would have to redesign processes are the least AI-fluent.
faktor_pembatal_transfer:
STRUCTURAL REASONS THE CHINESE VERSION WILL NEVER FULLY ARRIVE IN INDONESIA — and why the Indonesian outcome will be a different, in some ways worse, shape:

1) THE WHITE-COLLAR BASE IS TOO THIN. China's AI displacement is dramatic because it has an enormous formal white-collar economy — even at under 25% of a 725-million workforce, that is 150-180 million people in exactly the jobs agents automate. Indonesia has 59.93 million FORMAL workers total and 57.70% of all workers in the informal sector. There simply is not an Indonesian equivalent of 'tens of millions of office jobs' to eliminate. The absolute displacement will be an order of magnitude smaller. But the corollary is harsh: the jobs at risk are the SAME jobs that constitute Indonesia's only reliable ladder from tertiary education into the middle class. Small absolute numbers, catastrophic distributional significance.

2) NO MANUFACTURING BASE TO AUTOMATE. China's 30-million-job manufacturing decline (115m → <85m, 2013-2025) is inseparable from its 2-million-robot installed base and 392+ robot density. Indonesia's manufacturing is labour-intensive, low-margin (textiles, footwear, food processing) with robot density in the low tens, and its recent job losses (Sritex and the textile collapse) are about competitiveness and import pressure, NOT automation. The Chinese blue-collar automation story is largely inapplicable; Indonesia will lose manufacturing jobs to Chinese and Vietnamese automated factories abroad rather than to robots at home. This is displacement by TRADE, not by domestic AI.

3) NO STATE CAPACITY TO SUPPRESS OR ABSORB. China's model rests on instruments Indonesia does not have: layoffs above 10% requiring government approval; courts ruling AI substitution unlawful grounds for dismissal (three-plus cases, 260,000-yuan award); SOEs directed to absorb surplus labour; municipal subsidies of up to 29,000 yuan pushing graduates into delivery work; a civil-service exam channel absorbing millions of applicants. Indonesia's Cipta Kerja framework moved in the OPPOSITE direction — easier, cheaper dismissal. Indonesian displacement will therefore be faster, more visible, and less cushioned than China's.

4) THE INFORMAL SECTOR IS ALREADY THE ABSORBER, AND IT IS ALREADY FULL. China pushed displaced workers into a 280-million gig economy that had spare capacity for a while (until dozens of cities issued saturation warnings). Indonesia's informal sector at 57.70% is not a shock absorber with slack — it is the default state, with 47.42 million already non-full-time. Displaced graduates will not fall into gig work as a novel cushion; they will fall into an already-saturated ojol/informal market, driving down incomes for people who were already there. The distributional damage lands twice.

5) ARCHIPELAGIC GEOGRAPHY AND GRID CONSTRAINTS CAP DIFFUSION OUTSIDE JAVA. Compute, enterprise IT, and the white-collar workforce are overwhelmingly concentrated in Jabodetabek plus a handful of Java cities. There is no realistic path to a nationally uniform 90%-penetration outcome.

6) COST STRUCTURE INVERSION. In China, automating a 93,190-yuan office worker is obviously profitable. In Indonesia, a junior admin costs a fraction of that, and the fully loaded cost of an enterprise AI agent (licence + integration + local-language tuning + governance) can EXCEED the human's salary for several more years. Rational Indonesian firms will keep humans longer — which delays the shock but also delays the productivity gain, leaving Indonesia with neither the jobs China lost nor the output China gained.

7) NO DOMESTIC FRONTIER-MODEL INDUSTRY. China's displacement is at least paired with capturing the upside: DeepSeek, Qwen, Doubao, a 182-billion-yuan agent industry, and 74% growth in AI job postings. Indonesia will import the agents (largely from Chinese and US vendors) and export the value — absorbing the labour-market cost of AI without the compensating creation of an AI industry. This is the core asymmetry and the single most important policy problem.
tahun_masuk_indonesia: 2025-2026 — ALREADY ENTERING. Evidence that entry has begun: AI-attributed restructuring at ByteDance/Tokopedia, Shopee, and Lazada; Accenture and Salesforce cutting entry/mid-level roles globally with Indonesian exposure; AI agents commercially deployed in Indonesian banking, e-commerce, logistics (the Surabaya 75%-automation case) and priced at Rp1-2m/month; UI approving an AI undergraduate program (Oct 2025, intake 2026/2027); Komdigi's AI roadmap consultation (Aug 2025) and two draft Perpres targeted for Q1 2026; DPR Commission IX debating AI-displacement clauses in the Labor Law revision (2026); and — the clearest labour-market fingerprint — tertiary-graduate unemployment rising +23,085 YoY to 1,033,737 in Feb 2026 while national unemployment fell.
tahun_mainstream_indonesia: 2028-2030. Mainstreaming requires three conditions to converge: (a) AI-agent cost falling below Indonesian entry-level white-collar wages — plausible around 2027-2028 as inference costs continue to collapse; (b) enterprise digital maturity rising from ~23-26% to the 60-70% range, following the trajectory China took from roughly 2023 to 2026; (c) local compute capacity energised (the ~1.3 GW pipeline landing 2027-2029) plus better Bahasa Indonesia model performance. The most likely sequence: 2026-2027 quiet hiring freezes for entry-level admin, CS, content, and junior design roles; 2028 the first genuinely visible AI-attributed layoff wave in banking, telco, insurance, BPO and e-commerce; 2029-2030 mainstream, with 'AI-first' becoming the default operating assumption in large Indonesian corporates. [uncertain — projection]
tahun_puncak_indonesia: 2030-2033 for peak labour-market disruption. Reasoning: Indonesia's demographic bonus peaks around 2030 with the largest-ever cohorts of tertiary graduates entering the market at precisely the moment agent penetration in large corporates matures; the entry-level rung will be thinnest then. A secondary peak risk sits later (2032-2035) if global AI-driven reshoring and automated manufacturing abroad erode Indonesia's export-manufacturing employment simultaneously. Peak geography: Jabodetabek first and hardest (financial services, telco, e-commerce, professional services, creative agencies), then Surabaya, Bandung, Medan, Makassar. Peak sectors: BPO/shared services, banking back-office and CS, insurance claims processing, media and content production, advertising and design, legal and tax document processing, junior software QA. [uncertain — projection]
skenario_percepatan: Acceleration triggers, roughly in order of impact: (1) a sharp further fall in inference/agent cost — Rp1-2m/month dropping below ~Rp500k, putting agents inside UMKM budgets and below the cost of a junior staffer; (2) strong Bahasa Indonesia performance in an open-weight model (Qwen, DeepSeek, or a Sahabat-AI-type national model) removing the language barrier; (3) an economic shock or margin squeeze forcing cost-cutting — recession, rupiah stress, or an e-commerce profitability push, which converts optional automation into mandatory cost reduction; (4) the government adopting a Chinese-style adoption TARGET (an 'AI+ Indonesia' penetration goal) without the corresponding labour safeguards; (5) a single high-profile Indonesian corporate publicly proving large savings from agent deployment — the herd effect in Indonesian corporate governance is strong; (6) data-centre capacity energising ahead of schedule (Batam/Nvidia, Microsoft region) cutting latency and local inference cost; (7) aggressive Chinese vendor pricing — Alibaba Cloud and Huawei subsidising Qwen-based agents to win share, exactly as Chinese platforms subsidised their way into Indonesian e-commerce and payments; (8) BPO clients offshore mandating AI-first delivery in contracts, importing displacement directly into Indonesian delivery centres.
dampak_lapangan_kerja:
JOBS LOST OR SEVERELY COMPRESSED (highest exposure first). Tier 1 — near-certain compression by 2028-2030: first-line customer service and call-centre agents (routine, script-driven work is the most exposed segment globally; analysts project AI could affect up to half of all global contact-centre jobs by 2030); data entry and document verification clerks (the Surabaya logistics case already runs ~75% of verification without humans); administrative assistants and general back-office admin; junior content writers, copywriters, and SEO writers; junior graphic designers and 2D illustrators (~26% of illustrators already report lost work; Alibaba's Wan/'Happy Horse' video models are being marketed into Indonesia specifically for the creative industry); translators and localisation staff (~36% report lost work; China has already redesigned translation degrees so students 'direct and manage AI translators' rather than translate); basic bookkeeping and accounts-payable processing; junior QA/software testers and low-complexity coders; telemarketing; basic HR screening and recruitment coordination; paralegal document review; entry-level market research and report writing (Accenture explicitly cited data analysis, system testing, and report preparation as the automated functions reducing entry and mid-level need).
Tier 2 — partial task substitution, headcount thinning rather than elimination: junior financial analysts, insurance claims processors, radiology/pathology support roles, teaching support, mid-level project coordination, branch banking staff as digital channels absorb traffic.
Tier 3 — protected for now by cost structure or physical presence: skilled trades, healthcare delivery, logistics last-mile, construction, food service, agriculture, in-person sales, and anything requiring physical trust or regulatory presence.

THE ENTRY-LEVEL LADDER PROBLEM — the central mechanism. AI does not remove the senior professional; it removes the junior tasks that seniors used to be trained through. China's evidence is explicit: graduate postings -22% while AI-related postings rose 74%, and internationally, employment of 22-25 year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations fell about 13% relative to trend. Indonesia's Feb 2026 data already show this shape: national unemployment falling while tertiary-graduate unemployment rises to 1,033,737. The damage is not primarily mass firing; it is the destruction of the first rung, which delays or prevents entry into the formal economy entirely, and which no severance or unemployment-benefit regime addresses.

JOBS CREATED OR EXPANDED. AI/ML engineers, data engineers, MLOps; AI integration and agent-orchestration specialists; prompt and context engineers (transitional, likely absorbed into general professional skill by 2030); AI trainers, data annotators and evaluators (Indonesia has a genuine cost advantage here — a real export opportunity); AI governance, audit, risk and compliance officers (driven by the coming Perpres and sectoral rules); data-centre technicians, electrical and cooling engineers (the ~1.3 GW pipeline is a physical jobs pipeline); cybersecurity; robotics and automation technicians for the industrial segment; 'AI-native' small-business operators running one-person companies (the Alibaba 'Wukong' pattern); and the human-premium roles — complex negotiation, care work, high-trust advisory, creative direction, and anything where accountability must sit with a person. Net effect internationally is contested; McKinsey-type analyses project net creation, but for INDONESIA specifically the risk is that creation happens abroad (where the models are built) while displacement happens locally (where the agents are consumed).

SCALE CALIBRATION. Citi's China figure — 9.6% of jobs at high risk, 13.6% for people in their 20s — applied naively to Indonesia's ~145 million workers would imply ~14 million at risk, but this overstates it badly because Indonesia's automatable white-collar share is far smaller and its informal share far larger. A more defensible framing: the exposed population is concentrated in the roughly 60 million formal workers, and within that in urban service and office roles — plausibly 3-6 million jobs materially affected by 2030, with the sharpest effect on the ~1 million+ tertiary graduates entering the market each year. [uncertain — this is an analytical estimate, not a published figure]
dampak_kelas_menengah:
This trend attacks the Indonesian middle class at its point of formation rather than at its base. The Indonesian middle class has been shrinking for several years (widely reported contraction from roughly 57 million in 2019 to around 47-48 million by 2024, with the 'aspiring middle class' swelling) [uncertain — figures vary by definition and year], and the standard escalator out of that squeeze has been: tertiary degree → entry-level white-collar job in Jakarta or Surabaya → formal-sector income, BPJS coverage, mortgage and consumer credit eligibility. AI removes the middle step of that escalator specifically.

Concrete mechanisms: (1) DELAYED ENTRY. Tertiary-graduate unemployment at 6.13% against a national 4.68% and rising in absolute terms means the degree is already delivering worse-than-average labour-market outcomes; AI extends job-search duration, which in Indonesia usually means falling back on family support or informal work, delaying household formation, marriage, and property purchase. (2) WAGE COMPRESSION AT THE BOTTOM OF THE WHITE-COLLAR SCALE. When one AI-assisted junior does the work of three, firms hire one at a wage anchored to the old junior rate — real starting salaries stagnate while Jakarta living costs do not. China's version of this is graduates taking delivery work; Indonesia's version is graduates driving ojol, opening small online shops, or joining the freelance/gig market at rates the AI itself has undercut. (3) CREDENTIAL DEVALUATION. If the S1 no longer clears the path to formal employment, the household investment in tertiary education (a defining middle-class expenditure) loses its return, which is both an economic loss and a legitimacy shock. (4) THE PROFESSIONAL MIDDLE IS SQUEEZED FROM BOTH SIDES. Mid-career professionals in marketing, admin, HR, finance operations and creative services face task substitution without the retraining infrastructure to move up — Indonesia has no equivalent of China's US$15bn advanced-manufacturing retraining spend, and PwC's Indonesian data show the AI productivity gains concentrated in Gen Z while skill gaps persist across older cohorts, meaning the 35-50 cohort is the most exposed and least equipped. (5) COUNTERVAILING UPSIDE, UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED. The 33% of Indonesian workers already classed as advanced AI users stand to gain substantially — higher output, freelance leverage, access to global remote work, and the ability to run one-person businesses. The result is intra-middle-class polarisation: an AI-fluent upper-middle pulling away, and an AI-exposed lower-middle sliding toward informality.
dampak_daerah_non_jawa:
ASYMMETRIC AND, IN THE SHORT RUN, PROTECTIVE — but that protection is itself a form of exclusion.

Why non-Java is less exposed initially: the automatable white-collar employment base — corporate HQs, banking back-offices, BPO centres, digital agencies, professional services — is overwhelmingly concentrated in Jabodetabek, with secondary clusters in Bandung, Surabaya, Semarang, Medan, and Makassar. Regional economies outside Java are dominated by agriculture, mining and resource extraction, fisheries, plantation, trade, construction and public administration, none of which are near-term targets for AI agents. Informality is also higher outside Java, and informal work is by definition outside the digitised workflows agents automate.

Why that protection is not good news: (1) It reflects the ABSENCE of the very formal white-collar jobs regional graduates want. Regional tertiary graduates already face weaker local labour markets and migrate to Java for formal employment — AI shrinks exactly the Java-based entry-level pool they were migrating into, so the shock reaches non-Java regions through blocked out-migration and returning graduates rather than through local layoffs. (2) COMPUTE AND CAPABILITY CONCENTRATION WIDENS THE GAP. Data-centre capacity, cloud regions, and AI talent programs cluster in Java, Batam and Bali; the ~1.3 GW pipeline and the Nvidia/Microsoft/DAMAC investments create high-value technical jobs in a handful of locations. Alibaba Cloud's roadshow reach into Makassar, Aceh, Padang, and Papua is notable precisely because it is unusual — most AI capability-building stops at Java. (3) LANGUAGE AND DATA MARGINALISATION. Models perform worst in regional languages and on regional contexts, so AI services will be least useful where they are most needed, reinforcing a digital-capability divide. (4) THE ONE GENUINE REGIONAL OPPORTUNITY. Data annotation, AI training-data collection, local-language corpus building, and remote AI-assisted services are geographically footloose and could be deliberately sited in Yogyakarta, Malang, Makassar, Padang or Manado where costs are lower — this is the clearest policy lever for making AI a regional development tool rather than a Java-concentration tool. (5) POWER AND CONNECTIVITY REMAIN THE HARD CONSTRAINT: grid reliability and cost outside Java-Bali cap any serious compute decentralisation this decade.
jurusan_terancam:
Direct read-across from what China is actually closing (12,200 programs ended or suspended 2021-2025) plus Indonesian labour-market exposure:

HIGHEST RISK — programs whose core vocational output is now a model capability:
- Sastra/Bahasa Asing and Penerjemahan (foreign languages and translation). China's evidence is unambiguous: a May 2026 survey of 70 universities found 8 Japanese majors, 5 German majors and 5 translation programs eliminated; a 60-year-old Swahili translation course at a Chinese university was redesigned so students 'direct and manage AI translators'. In Indonesia ~36% of translators already report losing work. Sastra Inggris, Sastra Jepang, Sastra Mandarin, and D3/D4 Penerjemahan as currently taught are the single most exposed cluster.
- Sekretaris / Administrasi Perkantoran / Manajemen Perkantoran (D3) — the job the degree names is the job agents do first.
- Desain Komunikasi Visual and Desain Grafis at the production-skill level (~26% of illustrators report lost work). Note China's Communication University of China cut five programs including photography, comics, and visual communication design while adding 'Intelligent Imaging Art' — the lesson is redesign, not closure.
- Ilmu Komunikasi / Jurnalistik / Periklanan taught as content production rather than strategy, audience science, or verification.
- Akuntansi at the bookkeeping/processing level (D3 Akuntansi, entry-level AP/AR roles) — the analytical and assurance track survives; the processing track does not.

HIGH RISK — programs that survive only with substantial curricular change:
- Manajemen and Administrasi Bisnis taught as generic theory without data, analytics, or AI-tool fluency — Indonesia's single largest enrolment block and its most generic graduate output.
- Ilmu Perpustakaan/Kearsipan; D3 Perbankan and teller-track programs; Public Relations taught as press-release writing; Statistika/Matematika taught without computation; Teknik Informatika taught as syntax-level programming without systems, data, or ML depth (junior coding and QA are explicitly among the first automated).
- Hukum at the document-drafting and paralegal-review level (the advocacy, negotiation, and judgment core is safe).

CRITICAL CAVEAT — the real threat is not the field, it is the LEVEL. AI is removing junior TASKS, not whole professions. A translation graduate who becomes an AI-translation quality director is employable; one trained only to translate is not. The correct institutional response is the Chinese one — restructure the curriculum around directing, verifying, and being accountable for AI output — not mass closure. Indonesia should be far more cautious than China about eliminating humanities capacity outright, because verification, ethics, cultural judgment, and language stewardship become MORE valuable as generation becomes free.
jurusan_dibutuhkan:
TECHNICAL CORE: Artificial Intelligence / Kecerdasan Artifisial as a standalone undergraduate degree (UI's Fasilkom program, first intake 2026/2027; ITS Rekayasa Kecerdasan Artifisial; BINUS and UPH already running) — China went from 35 approved institutions in 2018 to 600+ universities with AI undergraduate programs by 2026, which is the scaling benchmark; Machine Learning Engineering and MLOps; Data Engineering (distinct from data science — Indonesian enterprises' binding constraint is un-digitised, unstructured data, not model availability); Data Science and applied statistics; Cybersecurity (agent deployment expands the attack surface); Cloud and distributed systems engineering.

THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE NEW CATEGORY — AI DEPLOYMENT AND ORCHESTRATION, not AI research. Indonesia will not build frontier models; it will integrate them. The scarce, well-paid, non-automatable skill is agent orchestration, systems integration, workflow redesign, evaluation, and accountability. Programs should be built around: AI product management, business-process redesign for agentic workflows, AI evaluation and quality assurance, and human-AI interaction design.

GOVERNANCE AND ASSURANCE — a genuine growth field created by regulation: AI governance, audit and compliance; AI ethics and policy; technology law (UU PDP, the incoming AI Perpres and sectoral derivatives, AI-content labelling/watermarking obligations); algorithmic accountability and model risk management for financial institutions.

PHYSICAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE — where the ~1.3 GW data-centre pipeline creates real jobs: data-centre engineering, electrical and thermal/cooling systems, power systems engineering, industrial automation and robotics technicians (China's model: robotics technicians, AI trainers, and cybersecurity professionals are the named growth roles alongside its automation build-out), embodied intelligence/robotics (9 Chinese universities were authorized for 'embodied intelligence' in the 2026 catalogue).

DOMAIN-PLUS-AI HYBRIDS — the highest-return combination for a country that imports models: AI in health and clinical informatics; agritech and precision agriculture (directly relevant outside Java); AI in mining, energy and geoscience; fintech and credit risk modelling; AI for logistics and maritime; AI in education. China's 2026 catalogue explicitly created 'AI for business' and 'data intelligence' as applied hybrids rather than pure CS variants — this is the model Indonesia should copy.

HUMAN-PREMIUM SKILLS THAT RISE IN VALUE: complex negotiation, sales and relationship management; care, health and education delivery; skilled trades and technical maintenance; creative DIRECTION (as distinct from creative production); verification, fact-checking, and information integrity; cross-cultural and multilingual judgment work; and any role where legal or professional accountability must attach to a named human.

STRATEGIC NICHE WITH EXPORT POTENTIAL: AI training-data services — annotation, evaluation, red-teaming, RLHF, and low-resource-language corpus construction for Bahasa Indonesia and regional languages. This is labour-intensive, geographically footloose, suited to Indonesia's cost structure and demographic bulge, and is one of very few ways Indonesia captures value from the AI stack rather than only paying for it.
china_education_response:
China has executed the fastest and most centrally directed higher-education restructuring of any major country in response to AI, and it is a direct policy template.

SCALE OF RESTRUCTURING: Between 2021 and 2025, Chinese universities ended or suspended approximately 12,200 undergraduate degree programs and introduced approximately 10,200 new ones — a churn of over 22,000 programs in five years, executed through the Ministry of Education's annual undergraduate major catalogue rather than through market attrition.

AI PROGRAM EXPANSION: AI undergraduate programs went from 35 approved institutions in 2018 to more than 600 universities by 2026. The MOE's 2026 catalogue added 38 new undergraduate majors effective for the 2026 gaokao intake, including AI for business (商业人工智能), embodied intelligence (具身智能), brain-computer science and technology, data intelligence, low-altitude economy management, semiconductor equipment engineering, and rare-earth science and engineering. Nine universities were specifically authorized to offer embodied intelligence. Eleven existing majors including Future Robotics and Interdisciplinary Engineering, plus four new ones, were for the first time placed under a new 'interdisciplinary studies' category — an explicit structural admission that AI-era fields do not fit the old disciplinary taxonomy. The 2025 catalogue had already added 29 new majors covering AI and frontier technologies.

WHAT IS BEING CUT: foreign languages and translation are the clearest casualties. A May 2026 survey of 70 universities found 8 Japanese-language majors, 5 German majors, and 5 translation studies programs eliminated, alongside broader foreign-language cuts. MyCOS, the main Chinese graduate-employment consultancy, notes that foreign-language majors were among China's fastest-growing programs for years and are now being forced to rethink their training model by AI translation tools.

CURRICULAR REDESIGN RATHER THAN PURE CLOSURE — the most transferable lesson: Communication University of China cut five programs (photography, comics, visual communication design among them) but simultaneously created 'Intelligent Imaging Art'. A 60-year-old Swahili translation course was redesigned so students learn to DIRECT AND MANAGE AI translators rather than translate themselves. The pattern is: keep the domain, move the human up the value chain to direction, verification, and accountability.

MECHANISM AND SPEED: this happened because China's MOE controls the national major catalogue and enrolment quotas, allowing annual, centrally-timed realignment of higher education to industrial policy — an instrument Indonesia's Kemendiktisaintek has in weaker form through prodi accreditation and quota approval.

WHAT CHINA IS ARGUABLY GETTING WRONG: the volume and speed of humanities and language cuts is already generating concern that China is eliminating exactly the interpretive, cultural, and verification capacity that becomes scarce when machine generation is free — and that 600+ AI programs will produce a glut of mediocre AI graduates chasing a smaller number of genuinely technical roles. Indonesia should copy the RESTRUCTURING MECHANISM and the DIRECT-THE-AI curricular philosophy, but not the scale of humanities elimination.
respons_kebijakan_china:
China's response is distinctive because it regulates the LABOR CONSEQUENCES of AI without slowing AI ADOPTION — the inverse of its 2020-2022 platform crackdown. The components Indonesia could adopt PREEMPTIVELY:

1) JUDICIAL DOCTRINE THAT AI SUBSTITUTION IS NOT LAWFUL GROUNDS FOR DISMISSAL. Chinese courts and labour arbitration have ruled in at least three cases that adopting AI does not by itself justify termination. A Beijing labour arbitration decision in December 2025 held that an employer must first consider contract modification, retraining, and internal transfer; one worker received 260,000 yuan (~US$38,000) for unlawful AI-substitution dismissal. This is the single most copyable instrument: it does not slow AI adoption, it simply reallocates the transition cost to the employer capturing the productivity gain.

2) ADMINISTRATIVE FRICTION ON MASS LAYOFFS. Chinese labour law requires government approval for layoffs exceeding 10% of a workforce; Beijing has reportedly directed large firms to avoid visible mass layoffs. The result is 'quiet layoffs' via attrition — slower, more manageable, though also less transparent.

3) A DEDICATED NATIONAL AI-EMPLOYMENT POLICY DOCUMENT. On 27 January 2026 MOHRSS announced China will issue a document on responding to AI's employment impact (应对人工智能影响促就业), bundled with: a 'stabilise, expand and upgrade employment' action; sectoral employment-support measures; a dedicated college-graduate and youth employment document; opinions on integrating urban and rural employment systems; Basic Rights Protection Measures for New Employment Form Workers; and Interim Regulations on Basic Rights Protection for Over-Age Workers. Under discussion: AI-specific unemployment insurance, 6-12 month grace periods before AI-driven layoffs take effect, mandatory upskilling funding, and regional employment-monitoring pilots.

4) EMPLOYMENT-RISK MONITORING AS INFRASTRUCTURE. Minister Wang Xiaoping's directive to build a statistical monitoring system covering key regions, industries, enterprises and groups, and to strengthen the mechanism for preventing and defusing large-scale unemployment risk with policy reserves and emergency response. This is early-warning capacity built BEFORE the crisis.

5) OFFICIAL DOCTRINE OF 'HUMAN-MACHINE COORDINATION' (人机协同). MIIT Vice-Minister Zhang Yunming: 'restructuring is not disappearance, iteration is not replacement.' Framing matters because it sets the legal and administrative default toward augmentation.

6) MASSIVE RETRAINING INVESTMENT: reportedly over US$15 billion in advanced-manufacturing retraining since 2020 [uncertain — single-source figure].

7) ABSORPTION CHANNELS AS DELIBERATE POLICY: SOEs directed to absorb surplus labour; local-government subsidies for hiring graduates; municipal subsidies up to 29,000 yuan pushing graduates into delivery work; expansion of graduate-school places and civil-service intake to delay labour-market entry.

WHAT INDONESIA CAN ADOPT PREEMPTIVELY, IN PRIORITY ORDER: (i) codify in the RUU Ketenagakerjaan that technological substitution alone is not a valid ground for PHK without a documented offer of retraining or redeployment — the highest-leverage, lowest-cost instrument; (ii) build the graduate-employment and AI-exposure monitoring system NOW, using BPS Sakernas plus job-board data, before the shock rather than after; (iii) require large employers to disclose AI-attributed headcount changes; (iv) attach a retraining levy or obligation to firms deploying agents at scale; (v) build the sectoral employment-support architecture in advance for the specific exposed sectors (BPO, banking back-office, creative services). Crucially, Indonesia has the rare option of legislating the safeguard BEFORE the displacement, which China did not.
rekomendasi_kebijakan_indonesia:
1) LEGISLATE THE SAFEGUARD BEFORE THE SHOCK — the core recommendation. Insert into the RUU Ketenagakerjaan revision an explicit provision that technological or AI-driven substitution is not, by itself, a lawful ground for PHK absent a documented offer of retraining, redeployment, or enhanced transition compensation. This mirrors the Chinese judicial doctrine (Beijing arbitration, Dec 2025; 260,000-yuan award) but arrives preemptively. DPR Commission IX (Pulung Agustanto) and Apindo are already discussing exactly this — the window is open in 2026 and closes once the shock lands.
2) BUILD AI-EXPOSURE LABOUR MONITORING NOW. Have BPS publish a quarterly AI-exposure series: entry-level vacancy counts by occupation, tertiary-graduate TPT disaggregated by field of study, time-to-first-job, and real starting salaries — plus a mandatory field in Kemnaker's PHK reporting capturing whether technology substitution was a cause. China built monitoring only as the shock hit; Indonesia can have the instrument ready by 2027.
3) DO NOT COPY THE 'AI+' PENETRATION TARGET WITHOUT THE LABOUR COUNTERWEIGHT. If Indonesia sets adoption targets, pair every diffusion target with a transition obligation. Adopting China's 70%/90% ambition without China's judicial and administrative brakes would produce the worst combination available.
4) MAKE THE PERPRES ENFORCEABLE ON THE LABOUR DIMENSION. The draft AI Perpres is reportedly sanction-free and governance-oriented; at minimum add a mandatory workforce-impact disclosure for large-scale AI deployment in regulated sectors (banking, telco, insurance, public services), and require human review and named accountability for automated decisions affecting employment or benefits.
5) FUND A NATIONAL RESKILLING INSTRUMENT WITH A REAL BUDGET LINE. Repurpose and expand Kartu Prakerja from a general voucher into a targeted AI-transition program with certified AI-deployment, data-engineering, and AI-governance tracks; consider a modest levy on large-scale enterprise AI deployment to fund it. Kemnaker is already using AI to map skill gaps and design training — connect that analytical capacity to actual funded programs.
6) CAPTURE PART OF THE STACK, DO NOT ONLY CONSUME IT. Tie data-centre incentives (the ~1.3 GW pipeline, Nvidia/Microsoft/DAMAC investments) to binding local-hiring, technology-transfer, and training commitments. Fund Bahasa Indonesia and regional-language corpora as public digital infrastructure so domestic models and evaluation services become viable, and deliberately build a national AI training-data and evaluation industry as an export sector.
7) PROTECT THE FIRST RUNG EXPLICITLY. Consider hiring incentives or wage subsidies tied specifically to fresh-graduate entry-level roles in AI-exposed occupations — the failure mode is not mass firing, it is the disappearance of the ladder. Any such scheme must be time-bound to avoid subsidising jobs that are genuinely obsolete.
8) GIVE KEMENDIKTISAINTEK AN ANNUAL PROGRAM-REALIGNMENT MECHANISM. China restructured 22,000+ programs in five years because MOE controls the national major catalogue. Indonesia should create a faster, evidence-driven prodi realignment cycle — but with a deliberate bias toward CURRICULAR REDESIGN over closure, and explicit protection for humanities capacity that becomes more valuable as generation becomes free.
9) PREPARE THE GIG/INFORMAL SAFETY NET FOR A SECOND WAVE. Displaced graduates will land in an ojol and informal market that is already saturated. Extend JKP eligibility toward platform and non-standard workers, and treat platform-worker protection (which China formalised for 200m+ workers) as connected policy, not a separate file.
10) REGIONAL DECONCENTRATION AS DESIGN, NOT HOPE. Site AI training-data operations, annotation centres, and AI skills academies deliberately outside Java (Makassar, Padang, Manado, Malang, Yogyakarta), and use Alibaba Cloud/Huawei/Telkom partnerships to require regional reach as a condition, extending the precedent of Alibaba Cloud's 9-city roadshow.
peluang_bisnis:

rekomendasi_individu_mahasiswa:
1) ASSUME THE ENTRY-LEVEL RUNG WILL BE MISSING, AND BUILD PROOF OF WORK THAT SUBSTITUTES FOR IT. The mechanism of harm is not being fired; it is never being hired. Portfolio, shipped projects, internships, freelance clients, and open-source or community contributions are now the entry credential — the transcript alone is not. Indonesian tertiary-graduate unemployment (6.13%) already exceeds the national rate (4.68%) and is rising in absolute terms.
2) BECOME THE PERSON WHO DIRECTS AND VERIFIES AI, NOT THE PERSON WHO COMPETES WITH IT. This is precisely how Chinese universities redesigned their translation programs — students learn to direct and manage AI translators. Whatever the domain, the durable skill is specification, evaluation, correction, and taking accountability for AI output.
3) STACK DOMAIN EXPERTISE + AI FLUENCY. Pure AI skills will commoditise; pure domain knowledge is exposed. The defensible position is domain-plus-AI: health + AI, agriculture + AI, law + AI, finance + AI, logistics + AI. China's own 2026 catalogue reflects this by creating 'AI for business' and 'data intelligence' rather than only more computer science.
4) LEARN DATA ENGINEERING AND SYSTEMS INTEGRATION, NOT JUST PROMPTING. Indonesian enterprises' binding constraint is messy, un-digitised data and unintegrated systems. The scarce, well-paid, non-automatable work is making organizational data usable and wiring agents into real workflows.
5) DEVELOP THE ACCOUNTABILITY SKILLS AI CANNOT HOLD: negotiation, client relationships, stakeholder management, judgment under ambiguity, and professional or legal responsibility. Roles where a named human must be answerable are structurally protected.
6) TREAT ENGLISH PLUS AI FLUENCY AS AN EXPORT LICENCE. Remote work for foreign employers is one of the few ways an Indonesian graduate escapes a compressed local entry-level market — and 33% of Indonesian workers are already advanced AI users, an unusual national advantage to build on.
7) GET CERTIFIED WHERE THE EMPLOYERS ARE LOOKING — cloud and AI certifications from Alibaba Cloud, AWS, Google, Microsoft; the Alibaba Cloud AI Talent Development Program and Telkom's AI Center of Excellence are free or low-cost local entry points.
8) CONSIDER THE PHYSICAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE TRACK. Data-centre engineering, power and cooling systems, industrial automation and robotics maintenance are growing (the ~1.3 GW pipeline), are non-offshorable, and face far less credential inflation than generic business degrees.
9) DO NOT ABANDON HUMANITIES CAPABILITY — REPOSITION IT. Verification, cultural judgment, ethics, and communication become scarcer and more valuable as machine generation becomes free. The failure mode is being a humanities graduate with no technical fluency; the winning position is a humanities graduate who can audit and direct AI systems.
10) BUILD AN INCOME FLOOR EARLY. Given a saturated ojol/informal market and delayed formal entry, freelance capability, a small AI-leveraged business, or a niche service practice is a rational hedge — the Alibaba 'Wukong' one-person-company pattern is directly available to Indonesian students today.
rekomendasi_perguruan_tinggi:

CROSS-CUTTING CURRICULAR REFORMS: (1) Make AI literacy a compulsory general-education course for every prodi, including non-technical ones — this is the single highest-return intervention. (2) Rewrite assessment: if an assignment can be completed by an agent, it no longer measures anything; move to oral defence, in-person work, process assessment, and critique of AI output. (4) Build employer co-design into curricula through the Telkom AI CoE, Alibaba Cloud, Huawei and Microsoft programs — but negotiate for genuine capability transfer and regional reach, not just vendor certification pipelines. (5) Establish tracer studies that specifically measure AI displacement of alumni — the sector currently has no visibility into its own obsolescence.
