dampak_negatif_china:
1) DESTRUCTION OF THE GRADUATE ENTRY PATHWAY. Graduate job postings fell 22% in H1 2025 while graduate job-seekers rose 8%, against record cohorts of 12.22 million (2025) and ~12.7 million (2026). Youth unemployment (16-24, ex-students) reached 16.3% in April 2026, near record. The social contract that a degree buys mobility has visibly broken.
2) DOWNWARD OCCUPATIONAL MOBILITY AND CREDENTIAL HUMILIATION. Graduates are absorbed into food delivery and gig work — cities have paid subsidies of up to 29,000 yuan to push new graduates into delivery, where a good day yields ~160 yuan against ~93,190 yuan/year for an average office job. Roughly a quarter of delivery riders now hold tertiary qualifications. This is a measurable waste of national human-capital investment and a documented source of individual despair.
3) 'QUIET LAYOFFS' AS A HIDDEN HARM. Because layoffs above 10% require government approval and firms are pressured to avoid visible cuts, displacement takes the form of attrition without backfill, performance-managed exits, forced transfers, and contractor non-renewal. Workers get less notice, less severance, and no public accounting. Alibaba's ~34% headcount decline in 2025, Baidu's ~7%, BYD's ~100,000, and headcount reductions at nearly half of all listed firms occurred with almost no formal redundancy process.
4) MASS PSYCHOLOGICAL STRESS. 'AI anxiety' reached ~7.8 million views as a hashtag on RedNote; the prevailing worker sentiment is captured by 'those who don't use AI will be eliminated'. This compounds an existing involution (内卷) and lying-flat (躺平) culture.
5) THE 30-MILLION MANUFACTURING JOB LOSS. Manufacturing employment fell from ~115 million (2013) to below ~85 million (2025) even as exports hit records — an automation-driven decoupling of output from employment that removed the historical absorption channel for less-educated workers.
6) DEFENSIVE INEFFICIENCY AND MISALLOCATION. As one fintech manager put it, 'private companies will need to make room for inefficiency to avoid mass layoffs.' Administrative suppression of layoffs converts a labour problem into a productivity and balance-sheet problem, with SOEs absorbing surplus labour they do not need.
7) HUMANITIES AND LANGUAGE CAPACITY DESTRUCTION. Eliminating Japanese, German, and translation programs at scale (and 12,200 programs overall) risks removing interpretive, cultural and verification capacity precisely when machine generation makes such capacity scarce — plus the near-term human cost to students and faculty in closed programs.
8) WAGE COMPRESSION AND EXPECTATION COLLAPSE. Engineering roles advertised at ~100,000 yuan/year and declining entry-level pay indicate that even 'safe' technical work is being repriced downward.
9) POLICY WHIPLASH RISK. The state is simultaneously demanding 90% AI penetration by 2030 and prohibiting AI-based dismissal — a contradiction firms resolve through opacity, which degrades the quality of the labour statistics the state relies on.
risiko_sosial_indonesia:
1) A LOST GRADUATE COHORT WITH NO ABSORPTION CHANNEL. Indonesia has China's problem without China's cushions. Tertiary-graduate unemployment is already 6.13% (1,033,737 people) and rising even as national unemployment falls; youth unemployment is 16.36%, essentially identical to China's 16.3%; NEET stands at ~8.9 million. But Indonesia has no SOE hiring capacity at Chinese scale, no civil-service exam absorbing millions, no municipal subsidies channelling graduates into delivery work, and a gig sector that is already saturated. If the entry-level rung disappears in 2027-2029, there is nowhere for that cohort to go.
2) FASTER, HARSHER, MORE VISIBLE DISPLACEMENT THAN CHINA'S. China's Cipta-Kerja-equivalent went the other way: Chinese courts treat AI substitution as unlawful dismissal grounds and require approval for large layoffs, while Indonesia's post-Cipta Kerja framework made dismissal cheaper and easier. Without an explicit statutory safeguard, Indonesian employers face far less friction in AI-attributed PHK.
3) DOUBLE-HIT INFORMALISATION. Displaced formal workers pushed into an informal sector already at 57.70% will compete with people already there, depressing incomes for the most vulnerable. BPS data already show more work shifting to the informal sector. The harm is regressive twice over.
4) HOLLOWING WITHOUT UPGRADING. China at least captured the upside — DeepSeek, Qwen, a 182-billion-yuan agent industry, 74% growth in AI job postings. Indonesia risks absorbing the labour-market cost while importing the technology, paying rent to foreign vendors, and creating few compensating high-value jobs. The 9-million talent gap against ~500,000 today means Indonesia is far better positioned to CONSUME agents than to BUILD them.
5) INTRA-CLASS POLARISATION AND SOCIAL RESENTMENT. The 33% of Indonesian workers who are advanced AI users will pull sharply ahead; the rest will not. Combined with an already-shrinking middle class and visible foreign ownership of the technology, this is fertile ground for economic nationalism and anti-technology politics — the #TolakGambarAI illustrator backlash is an early, small-scale example.
6) REGULATORY VACUUM DURING THE CRITICAL WINDOW. The draft AI Perpres is reportedly sanction-free; the RUU Ketenagakerjaan revision is unresolved. If the shock lands in 2027-2028 with no statutory retraining or redeployment obligation, the transition cost falls entirely on workers.
7) CREATIVE-SECTOR COLLAPSE AT THE ENTRY LEVEL. With roughly 26% of illustrators and 36% of translators already reporting lost work, and Alibaba Cloud actively marketing Wan/'Happy Horse' video models into the Indonesian creative industry, the junior tier of a sector Indonesia had positioned as a growth area (ekonomi kreatif) may be eliminated before it matures.
8) EDUCATION-SYSTEM MISMATCH BECOMING PERMANENT. Universities producing 100,000-200,000 digital talents a year against a need for 9 million by 2030, while continuing to graduate large volumes into the most exposed generic programs, converts a temporary mismatch into a structural one.
9) DATA, SURVEILLANCE AND GOVERNANCE RISKS from AI agents deployed in HR, credit, and public-service decisions without meaningful sanction or appeal rights under the current draft framework.
10) FISCAL AND SOCIAL-PROTECTION STRAIN: JKP and BPJS coverage are calibrated to formal-sector job loss, not to a cohort that never enters formal employment at all — the safety net misses precisely the population most affected.
unintended_consequences:
OBSERVED IN CHINA: (1) Suppressing layoffs administratively produced 'quiet layoffs' that are worse for workers — no notice, no severance, no public record — and simultaneously degraded the reliability of official employment statistics; the headline urban unemployment rate stayed near 5% while the underlying entry-level market collapsed. (2) Firms began deliberately preserving inefficiency to avoid triggering approval thresholds, converting a labour problem into a productivity drag. (3) The graduate-to-delivery-rider pipeline created a highly educated gig workforce, which then made platform-labour conditions a politically explosive issue and forced a separate regulatory intervention for 200m+ platform workers. (4) Explosive growth to 600+ university AI programs risks producing an AI-graduate glut chasing a much smaller pool of genuinely technical roles — credential inflation reproducing itself one field over. (5) Cutting 12,200 programs including language and translation may have destroyed verification and cultural-judgment capacity that becomes scarcer as generation becomes free. (6) DeepSeek's own public statement that AI success means 'replacing the vast majority of human jobs' undermined the government's 'human-machine coordination' messaging and amplified public anxiety — the industry's candour worked against the state's framing. (7) AI-related postings rose 74% while overall graduate postings fell 22%, producing a labour market that is simultaneously desperately short of talent and full of unemployed graduates.

PREDICTED FOR INDONESIA: (1) AI may INCREASE measured employment in the short run by enabling more one-person businesses and freelancers, masking the destruction of stable formal entry-level jobs behind a rising count of precarious self-employment. (2) Cheap AI agents may extend the life of low-productivity Indonesian firms rather than raise productivity — automating around bad processes instead of fixing them, so Indonesia gets the job losses without the growth. (3) The talent shortage may perversely SLOW displacement: firms cannot deploy agents they cannot configure, so Indonesia's weakness becomes a temporary shield — and a permanent handicap. (4) Universities may over-rotate into AI programs, producing a glut of mediocre AI graduates while the actual scarce skills are data engineering, integration, and governance. (5) Preemptive labour regulation, if written clumsily, could push AI deployment offshore — Indonesian firms buying automated services from foreign providers rather than automating domestically, exporting the jobs entirely. (6) Data-centre investment may deliver far fewer jobs than the headline dollar figures imply (data centres are capital- not labour-intensive) while consuming scarce grid capacity, generating disappointment and backlash. (7) Because AI arrives via foreign vendors, a labour backlash could take an economic-nationalist form aimed at Chinese and US technology firms rather than at the displacement mechanism itself. (8) Remote work may become the escape valve for the AI-fluent 33%, producing a brain drain of exactly the people needed to build domestic capability.
kelompok_rentan:
1) FRESH TERTIARY GRADUATES, ESPECIALLY IN GENERIC PROGRAMS — the primary victims. 1,033,737 D4/S1/S2/S3 holders already unemployed (TPT 6.13% vs 4.68% national), a figure that rose +23,085 YoY even as national unemployment fell. Most exposed: manajemen, administrasi, akuntansi (processing track), komunikasi, sastra/bahasa, DKV, and non-elite informatics graduates. They face a market where the first rung is being removed.
2) WOMEN IN ADMINISTRATIVE AND CLERICAL ROLES — administrative assistants, secretaries, data entry, and first-line customer service are disproportionately female in Indonesia and sit at the very top of the automation-exposure list. This is a gendered shock that current policy discussion has not addressed.
3) BPO, CALL-CENTRE AND SHARED-SERVICES WORKERS — the segment where routine, script-driven work is most exposed; analysts project AI could affect up to half of global contact-centre jobs by 2030, and the Philippines has already downgraded its 2028 BPO employment projection from 2.5 million to as low as 1.85 million. Indonesia's smaller BPO sector faces the same physics.
4) JUNIOR CREATIVE WORKERS AND FREELANCERS — illustrators (~26% reporting lost work), translators (~36%), junior copywriters, video editors, and entry-level designers. Freelancers have no severance, no JKP, and no collective representation, and are being directly targeted by vendor marketing of generative video and image models into Indonesia.
5) MID-CAREER WORKERS AGED 35-50 IN WHITE-COLLAR SUPPORT ROLES — PwC's Indonesian data show the AI productivity gain concentrated in Gen Z with persistent skill gaps in older cohorts. This group has financial obligations (mortgages, children's education), the least AI fluency, and the weakest access to reskilling.
6) EXISTING INFORMAL AND GIG WORKERS — the second-order victims. They will absorb the displaced without any increase in demand, so ojol and informal incomes fall for people who were already the most precarious. Indonesia's informal share is 57.70% and 47.42 million workers are already non-full-time.
7) REGIONAL AND NON-JAVA GRADUATES — insulated from local AI displacement only because there were never many formal white-collar jobs locally; their route to mobility was migration to Java, which is exactly the pathway being narrowed.
8) STUDENTS CURRENTLY ENROLLED IN PROGRAMS BEING OBSOLETED — those two or three years into translation, secretarial, or production-design degrees have already sunk the investment and cannot easily switch; China's program closures show how fast institutions move once the shift is recognised.
9) LOW-SKILL FORMAL WORKERS IN LABOUR-INTENSIVE MANUFACTURING — not directly automated in Indonesia, but exposed to displacement-by-trade as Chinese and Vietnamese automated production (2m+ robots, 392+ density) undercuts Indonesian textile and footwear employment; the Sritex collapse is the template.
10) PEOPLE WITH LIMITED ENGLISH AND LOW DIGITAL LITERACY — locked out of the AI-fluent 33% and out of the remote-work escape valve, in a market where model performance in Bahasa Indonesia and regional languages remains weaker.
kasus_china:

Baidu (~-7%) and BYD (~-100,000, ~10%) show the same pattern; nearly half of all listed Chinese firms cut headcount in 2025.

CASE 3 — THE MICRO-DRAMA STUDIO COLLAPSE. Entertainment and micro-drama production departments reported shrinking from 30-40 people to about 10 after AI adoption — a ~70-75% reduction in a single function. This is the most concrete Chinese evidence of what generative video and content models do to creative-sector employment, and it is directly relevant to Indonesia because Alibaba Cloud is marketing the same class of models (Wan, 'Happy Horse') into the Indonesian creative industry.

CASE 4 — THE BEIJING AI-DISMISSAL ARBITRATION (DECEMBER 2025). Labour arbitration held that adopting AI is not valid grounds for termination and that employers must first consider contract modification, retraining, and internal transfer; across at least three cases Chinese courts have ruled against AI-substitution dismissals, with one worker awarded 260,000 yuan (~US$38,000). This established the world's first meaningful judicial doctrine allocating AI transition costs to the employer capturing the gain — the single most copyable instrument for Indonesia.

CASE 5 — MOHRSS, 27 JANUARY 2026. At a regular press conference the Ministry announced China would issue a dedicated document on responding to AI's employment impact, alongside a stabilise-expand-upgrade employment action, sectoral support measures, a graduate/youth employment document, and basic-rights protections for new-form and over-age workers, with Minister Wang Xiaoping directing the build-out of unemployment-risk monitoring across key regions, industries, enterprises and groups. This is the first time a major economy formally opened an AI-specific labour policy file.

CASE 6 — THE EDUCATION PIVOT. 600+ universities with AI undergraduate programs by 2026 (from 35 institutions in 2018); 12,200 programs ended or suspended and 10,200 introduced over 2021-2025; 38 new majors in the 2026 catalogue including embodied intelligence and AI for business; and a 60-year-old Swahili translation course redesigned so students direct and manage AI translators rather than translate. Kemnaker recorded 88,000+ layoffs in 2025 and 23,470 in January-May 2026.
- MICRO-DRAMA STUDIO COLLAPSE → Indonesia's creative-sector damage: ~26% of illustrators and ~36% of translators reporting lost work, the #TolakGambarAI backlash, and Alibaba Cloud actively marketing Qwen, Wan and 'Happy Horse' generative models to the Indonesian creative industry across a 9-city roadshow.
- AGENT DEPLOYMENT → the Surabaya national logistics firm running ~75% of document verification, delivery scheduling and complaint handling without human intervention; AI agents priced at Rp1-2 million/month with WhatsApp-native deployment now inside UMKM budgets; Bank Mandiri applying AI to efficiency and risk while explicitly declining near-term headcount reduction — the clearest signal that Indonesia is at the deployment-without-displacement stage China passed through in 2023-2024.
- JUDICIAL DOCTRINE → no Indonesian equivalent yet. No known PHI ruling on AI-substitution dismissal. This is the most important missing piece.
- MOHRSS POLICY FILE → Komdigi's two draft Perpres (National AI Roadmap 2026-2030 and AI Ethics/Governance), targeted for Q1 2026 and reportedly sanction-free; DPR Commission IX (Pulung Agustanto) arguing the Labor Law revision must protect workers from automation and AI; Apindo pushing the RUU Ketenagakerjaan toward job creation and PHK prevention; Kemnaker using AI for labour-market analysis and training design (webinar 17 July 2026). Indonesia is debating labour safeguards at roughly the same time as China but BEFORE the shock — a genuine timing advantage.
- EDUCATION PIVOT → UI Fasilkom's AI undergraduate program (Senate approval 3 Oct 2025, first intake 2026/2027, ~16 designated lecturers), ITS Rekayasa Kecerdasan Artifisial, BINUS and UPH AI programs — a handful of institutions versus China's 600+, and no national program-realignment mechanism comparable to the MOE catalogue.
- ABSORPTION CHANNEL → Indonesia's ojol/informal sector (57.70% informality, 47.42 million non-full-time) is the analogue of China's 280-million gig economy, but it is already saturated and has no equivalent of the 29,000-yuan graduate subsidy.

catatan_kontradiksi_data:
1) DID AI CAUSE THE CHINESE LAYOFFS? Directly contradicted in-source. Professor Sun Zhongwei argues the headcount cuts are 'much more about adjusting to a downturn after that cycle of growth than being about AI displacing jobs,' and headhunter Claire Deng says 'I don't think AI has had a systemic impact yet — it's still quite fragmented.' Against this, the same reporting documents micro-drama departments collapsing from 30-40 people to ~10 and a fintech firm replacing marketing and front-end roles with AI. Most defensible reading: AI is an accelerant and a justification layered on top of a post-internet-boom correction, not yet the primary cause.
2) ENTRY-LEVEL POSTINGS — DIRECT CONTRADICTION. Zhaopin reports graduate-targeted postings down 22% in H1 2025, while BOSS Zhipin reports entry-level postings holding steady at ~7% of listings. These are different metrics (absolute graduate-targeted volume vs entry-level share of all listings) and different platforms, but the divergence is large enough that the -22% figure should not be treated as a settled national statistic.
3) HEADLINE UNEMPLOYMENT VS THE UNDERLYING MARKET. China's urban surveyed unemployment sits stably near 5% (below the 5.5% target) with ~3 million jobs added in Q1 2026, while youth unemployment is 16.3% and graduate postings collapsed. The headline series is not capturing the phenomenon — a caution that applies equally to reading Indonesia's falling 4.68% national TPT while tertiary-graduate unemployment rises.
4) AI-AGENT MARKET SIZE — WIDE DIVERGENCE. 182.34bn yuan (2025, Guanyan) vs 212bn yuan (2025, enterprise-grade) vs projections ranging from 852bn yuan (2028) to 3.32 trillion yuan (2029). CAGRs quoted between 72.7% and 107%. These are vendor and consultancy estimates with incompatible definitions of what counts as the 'agent market'.
5) INDONESIAN AI-ADOPTION FIGURES ARE MUTUALLY INCONSISTENT. APJII says 18.2% population adoption; Microsoft says 33% of workers are Frontier Professionals (double the global average); PwC says 69% have used AI for work but only 16% daily; Pertama Partners says ~26% organizational implementation; IBM/Advisia says 23% of enterprises are at the investment stage. One source cites '92% adoption' [almost certainly a vendor-marketing figure and not credible]. These measure different populations and different intensities and must not be compared directly.
6) THE '>160,000 INDONESIAN TECH WORKERS LAID OFF IN 2026' FIGURE almost certainly reflects a GLOBAL tech-layoff tracker rather than Indonesian layoffs; Kemnaker's own national figures are 88,000+ (all of 2025, all sectors) and 23,470 (Jan-May 2026). Do not use the 160,000 figure as an Indonesian statistic.
7) CREATIVE-SECTOR JOB-LOSS PERCENTAGES (26% of illustrators, 36% of translators) appear in Indonesian media without a clearly identified survey population; they may be international figures circulated locally. Treat as directional only.
8) UNEMPLOYMENT TOTALS FOR INDONESIA differ across reports (7.24 million vs 7.35 million) because of different reference periods (February vs later 2026 releases) — always cite the reference month.
9) CHINA'S POLICY POSTURE IS INTERNALLY CONTRADICTORY BY DESIGN: the State Council mandates 90% AI penetration by 2030 while courts rule AI substitution an unlawful ground for dismissal and MIIT insists 'iteration is not replacement.' Both are real policy; firms resolve the tension through opacity, which degrades data quality.
10) TOKOPEDIA'S JULY 2026 '90% LAYOFF' CLAIM was a social-media rumour; the verified figure was roughly 200 employees accepting packages. Widely circulated Indonesian layoff numbers require verification against Kemnaker or company filings.
11) INDONESIA'S INTERNET PENETRATION (81.72%) EXCEEDS CHINA'S (80.1%), which cuts against the intuitive assumption of a large technology lag and is the strongest single reason to compress lag estimates for software-delivered automation relative to prior China-to-Indonesia trends.
